subtopic: YUKON MINERALS ACT
subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION, ACQUISITION AND RECORDING OF CLAIMS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of features of Bill C-187, the Yukon Minerals Act, which disturb me greatly, and chief amongst them is the excessive amount of discretionary powers which will be vested in appointed officials of the public service in the administration of this act. The dangers of these powers, quite aside from them being discretionary, lie in the fact that appeals to independent judicial bodies from decisions made under them do not exist.
Over 40 years ago the Right Hon. Lord Hewart of Bury, Lord Chief Justice of England, wrote an incisive and still timely work called "The New Despotism". One of the chapters in his book is entitled "Administrative Lawlessness", from which I would like to quote the following passage:
Will anybody at this time of day deny that it is essential to the proper administration of justice that the decision should be based on evidence, and that the evidence should be heard in the presence of both parties, who are given the opportunity of cross examination? Evidence not tested by cross examination is nearly always misleading and practically valueless. The public official, as had been observed, may, and often does, decide without any evidence at all, and he may act on ex parte statements, made by one party without anything to support them, which are never brought to the knowledge of the other party, so that he has no opportunity to contravert them. Is it too much to say that such proceedings are a mere travesty of justice?
Earlier on in his work, Lord Hewart observed that:
To employ the terms "administrative law" and "administrative justice" to such a system, or negation of system, is really grotesque. The exercise of arbitrary power is neither law nor justice, administrative or at all. The very conception of law is a conception of something involving the application of known rules and principles, and a regular course of procedure.
Subclause (1) of clause 37 of Bill C-187 provides for the supervising mining recorder to cancel the recording of, or to refuse to record, any mineral claim where he is satisfied that the person claiming the rights involved therein is not entitled to them. While an appeal from his decision is permitted, it is restricted to being heard by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), whose decision thereon then becomes final. When we remember that the minister will be entirely dependent on the advice of his officials in arriving at the decisions made on such appeals, it becomes obvious that, in effect, what is taking place is really a meaningless appeal procedure whereby one public servant, or several, pass judgment on the appropriateness of the decision of one of their colleagues. Under these circumstances, can any one wonder why miners are apprehensive about the type of justice which they are likely to receive under the provisions of this bill? Public servants, passing judgment on other public servants, particularly when they are all in the same department, in my view represent nothing more than the workings of a mutual admiration society.
April 26, 1971

As a further specific example of excessive discretionary powers proposed in the bill, Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to clause 79(2), a particularly important clause because it deals with annual royalties payable to the Crown by mine owners. This subclause allows the minister-and of course this authority will be delegated-to decide whether two or more mines are operated by the same mine operator, or whether they are under the same general management and control. There is no appeal provided from this most arbitrary decision, the consequences of which could be enormous for the people who may be affected by it.
Paragraph (a) of clause 83 empowers the minister to reduce the value of depreciation on machinery, equipment or buildings at a mine where such depreciation has been claimed at a rate of 15 per cent per annum. Again, no appeal lies from this arbitrary decision. The discretionary powers embodied in the bill only add uncertainty to the Yukon mining industry, an industry which if nothing else is uncertain and risky by its very nature. Hon. members also ought to note that the proposed legislation further threatens the industry by establishing a most substantially increased scale of royalties which will not be alleviated by tax abatement provisions because, as I pointed out in my remarks on April 22, the Yukon Territory is not a province.
The measures proposed in this bill are particularly resented by the people of the Yukon Territory because, at a time when mining development is just beginning to move at a very encouraging rate, new proposals are introduced which place mineral operations in the Yukon Territory at a very significant taxation disadvantage compared with the same type of operation in British Columbia and Quebec. This cannot but discourage mineral exploration and development in the Yukon Territory, with appropriate consequences for the people who live there.
In a recent report in the Globe and Mail, to be specific on March 26, 1971, Mr. Jack Austin, the Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, is reported as having told a group of mining executives in Toronto that:
Old antagonisms between government and the mining industry are breaking down.
If the present bill, as proposed, becomes law I can assure Mr. Austin and his minister, as well as the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, that they will be in for very substantial disillusionment. How can a piece of legislation such as the present bill, which would treat so unfairly the principal industry in an area faced with enormous natural problems in developing industrially, be received with anything else but hostility by the people who must operate under it or who otherwise will be affected by it?
In response to Mr. Austin's questionable optimism, I think it is worth citing a small portion from an editorial entitled "This is Where It's At" which appeared in the December, 1970, edition of the Western Miner. The final paragraph in that editorial reads:
As Mr. P. M. Reynold, President of Bethlehem Copper Corporation, so aptly observed at a recent meeting with Finance
Yukon Minerals Act
Minister Benson-"We are just not able to communicate with you and your advisers. We are not on the same wave length." The industry has made every possible effort to communicate, but apparently to no avail. Surely, with such undeniable evidence of the employment creating capability of the mining industry, government must reconsider its proposals to destroy this capability through unrealistic tax policies.
If we were dealing with a government which had a normal measure of humility, it might be possible to have some of the more extreme and punitive aspects of this legislation changed. Frankly, having observed the arrogance and self-righteousness of the government, particularly when it comes to listening to points of view alternative to its, I must despair of hoping that it will heed the representations which have been made against the proposed act by such bodies as the Vancouver Board of Trade.
In its letter of February 23, 1971, the Vancouver Board of Trade wrote to the minister as follows:
It is calculated that the proposed Yukon royalty will be more than three times as much as the present royalty over the first five years of an operating mine and more than twice as much over the first ten years.
This increase in disparity with mining taxes in the provinces coupled with the higher cost of mining and exploration in the Yukon will minimize the future growth in the territory.
On the matter of ministerial discretion, the Board of Trade observed, and again I quote:
There are sufficient uncertainties in mining without compounding the problem. Ministerial discretion, which in practice may mean a civil servant without mining or business experience, is an unacceptable method of applying a tax. It should be used as a last resort and not to cover vagueness and ambiguity in drafting. Examples of unnecessary use of ministerial discretion can be found throughout the bill but in particular we point out section 79(2), 80(c) and 83(a) and 84. The abrogation of parliamentary rights and the resultant possible abuse becomes critical when a taxpayer has no right of appeal to a court.
The Yukon Chamber of Mines in its submission to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development on this bill made the following criticism of its royalties provisions:
The Finance Minister's white paper on tax reform indicates a major tax increase for mining companies. A study of an existing copper mining company of an average size revealed that over a ten year period its tax burden would have been increased by more than 35 per cent had the white paper been in effect during that time. In a ten year period the total tax burden for a mining company operating in British Columbia under the white paper would have been 60 per cent greater than the burden it would have had to bear in the United States and 63 per cent more than it would have had to sustain in Australia. Mining investment capital is very specialized in that it tends to stay with the industry and not move to other industries. Should mining in Canada become less attractive as a result of the white paper it is very probable that Canadian mining capital would not be deployed to some other activity in Canada but rather would leave the country in search of other more attractive (mining) ventures.
It seems to me that once again the government is working at cross purposes in this bill. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) is responsible for a department which is spending many millions of dollars yearly in an effort to stimulate economic expansion in areas where such activity is not taking place at a sufficient rate and in a degree to provide stable

April 26, 1971
Yukon Minerals Act
employment tor the local work force. The provisions of this bill will work to the detriment of the efforts of his department in giving incentive grants to industries located in the north because its provisions will work in such a way as to discourage and penalize development in the principal industry in the Yukon Territory. Those of us who have watched the progress of mineral development at such an optimistic rate in the Yukon Territory have hoped that from it would spring logically related, and badly needed secondary industries to provide a whole new base for future development in that part of our country.
There is no doubt, however, that short-sighted, negative, arbitrary and restrictive measures, such as those contained in this proposed act, will destroy any such hope for the development of secondary industries when the primary industry on which they would be based will be so adversely affected by this unwarranted piece of legislation. Is it any wonder that it has been so soundly criticized by those people who know best the needs of the Yukon Territory and whose views I have already cited in small measure earlier in this speech? This proposed act is merely further evidence that the government intends to continue its policy of designing laws geared to making life simple for the bureaucrats. The fact that this measure is neither sought by the people whom it affects, nor of benefit to them, is not, of course, and as usual, regarded by this government as being sufficient reason for altering it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I prepared this speech about a month and a half ago, so if the situation regarding the bill has changed in the meantime I hope I can still be understood. I should like to suggest that the minerals or anything else in the north should be developed for the benefit of the people of all Canada. Perhaps we should start with the people of the north and then include all Canada, but I do not think these resources should be developed only for the people of southern Canada, as I am afraid has been the case quite frequently in the past.
I think there should be some definite move on the part of the government, in connection with this bill or any other, to help the people of the north on a permanent basis. I cannot think of anything that would be more effective than moving those people connected with the administration of mining or power or anything else to the communities concerned. Surely, if they lived in the area they would have a better understanding of the problems and their decisions would benefit the people much more than decisions made in Ottawa.
The complaints I receive from people in the north tend to be along the line that we do not understand their problems and make decisions about things without sufficient knowledge. I would like, therefore, to suggest that the government base its decision-making personnel closer to the areas with which they are concerned. We should make definite efforts to conserve the non-renewable resources of the north for future use. It will be too bad if we do not make the most effective use of the resources
available. First, we should take an inventory of the mineral resources of the north. We have done this to some degree already in the Carr report, which resulted from a study of the obvious things in the north but I am sure there is still much to be done.
I should like to make the following points: There has been no study of Canada's mineral resources either in the north or in the rest of Canada, or of our future national needs for various minerals similar to the study of the National Energy Board on oil, gas and coal in which the future demand and supply reserves were estimated based on probable reserves, projected future production, and future needs based on certain estimates of what our economic growth, industrial development and trading patterns should be. As far as mineral resources are concerned, the Canadian government is pursuing a "head in the sand" type of policy in which it is assumed that we have plentiful reserves and our economic growth and balance of payments position depend upon the ever-increasing development and sale of our natural resources by whomever can be enticed into exploiting them.
I would suggest that it is important that we make an inventory of what we have, and then decide on our future needs. Exploiting our resources to make money is not good enough. In conjunction with the mining development in the north, we should begin to build secondary industries. Smelters, refineries and reduction plants would provide a base for heavy industry, and freight costs on many items in and out would be reduced if we had a total package rather than one primary industry. The development of a total economy, rather than just mining, is desirable. It should not just be a matter of mine quickly, get out and leave the north. Mining will form the basis of northern economy but development of support services may bring something which will be renewable and long lasting. I would suggest also the development of farming. Thinking in terms of the Yukon, there may be a form of farming, different from that in Ontario or western Canada, but which would be suitable to that particular area.
I have asked the minister a number of times if he has investigated what the Russians have done. I have suggested that he take the committee to see how they have developed the north. As I understand it, the Canadian government has not done too much. I am sure the committee would gain much from such a visit and could make worth-while recommendations as a result. I saw a film provided by the minister called "Below Zero". It was most enjoyable but I noticed a serious omission. There was nothing in it about the country which has more northern territory and more winter than all others put together, that is Russia. Surely, this area should be investigated. I do not suggest that we should do everything the way the Russians do or that they have necessarily done the right thing, but surely we could learn something from them.
I read Farley Mowat's book on Siberia recently and while I do not suggest that he is an authority on this or any other north, he did point out some measures that I do not think we have followed in Canada. He spoke of using the permafrost to build dams, for instance, and this

April 26, 1971

idea interested me very much. He described some testing in regard to pipelines, and mentioned mining for diamonds and gold and drilling for oil. He described support services such as agriculture in the north, speaking particularly of reindeer herds which supply meat for people in the mining camps. Surely, it would be worth while for the committee to make a trip to northern Siberia in order to study what has been done there. I do not think the minister or members of the committee have been able to persuade the government to let them go. Should they be able to do so, I am sure there would be no lack of volunteers from this side of the House to accompany them. In so far as this bill is concerned, I think we should certainly make a trip to the north to hear what the people there think about it.
With regard to ownership in the north, I should like to make the brief comment that, in developing mines in the north beyond the financial capacity of Canadian private enterprise, rather than introduce foreign capital we should adopt the Panarctic approach. Further, if we want to construct smelters or refineries and things of that kind, we should turn to the Canada Development Corporation for financing. After all, why ship out of the country minerals in unprocessed form if we can process them at home? I suggest here is a logical place for the Canada Development Corporation to assist in Canadian development. Finally, we should show particular concern for the natives of the north. We should educate them so that they can contribute to northern development and find employment in the mining of Yukon minerals.

May I thank all hon. members who have participated in the debate, which I think has been a good one. Some hon. members wanted to raise other problems that have arisen in the past, such as the problems facing our native peoples. I am sorry we cannot have a full discussion of those problems, but I would say that I think all hon. members, certainly those on this side of the House, will agree that never before has the federal government entered into a dialogue with the native population of Canada. We have tried to seek their advice concerning the many measures we are proposing, especially in the field of employment in the north. We started a campaign two years ago to try to persuade developers in the north to give priority to the employment of the native popula-
Yukon Minerals Act
tion. This was evident from the guidelines we issued last August which stated that, if pipelines are constructed in the north, not only at the construction stage but at the operation stage the native people should be fully and permanently employed.
We very strongly believe that if we give our native people the skills required they will make very good employees and be very reliable. There is one benefit we will all gain from their working in the north, and that is that they will have no wish to come south. They are happy to live in the north because that is their country. The government and I realize this, and it is why we are not shy about speaking of what we have done and are planning to do for our native people.
Now is not the time to discuss this because this bill deals with mineral development in the Yukon. It is not a perfect bill, of course, and I said in my speech that we would make some changes at the committee stage. People in the north are concerned about the level of royalties, and I did say that we would make some adjustments there. I think all hon. members will agree that we must make sure that the royalties we receive from the mines in the north are not higher in amount than those received in British Columbia. But I repeat: We are going to make sure that revenue from royalties from mines in the Yukon received by the government will be lower than revenues received by the provincial administration of B.C. In this regard, I am going to present an amendment that will reflect the wishes of the House.
As far as the Canadian participation clause is concerned, I do not apologize for forcing industry in the north to accept investment from Canadians. This is the only industry in the Yukon under federal administration to which a clause of this sort does not apply. Pending a general review of policy on Canadian participation; we are going to put this proposal forward. I do not think development of the Yukon will suffer. At the same time, I think it is right that Canadians be allowed to participate in northern development if they so wish.

speechtext:
that Bill C-288, to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a little later in the session I will be bringing in, I hope, changes to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act which have been awaited for some considerable time by members of the House who are interested in the problems of labour, and by organized labour itself. I think, however, we tend to forget that in Canada only about 40 per cent of the work force may be considered to be organized, that is, represented by trade unions at the bargaining table, and about 50 per cent in the federal field due primarily to the fact that public servants in general are entitled to collective bargaining.
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
When we do bring forward the bill on the IRDI Act later in the session I think we will have indicated, despite the criticism that all too frequently is raised in respect of collective bargaining these days, that we do believe this Canadian system bears perhaps strengthening but certainly warrants preserving. I think it goes without saying that in a civilized system the responsibility of government does not end with providing the legal framework within which organized labour and management bargain to establish their norms. I believe it is the responsibility of the government to protect the unorganized in this country who, as I mentioned, represent the greater percentage of the work force. I refer to people who are not covered by collective agreements and depend, therefore, on the federal government and provincial governments to varying degrees to provide the standards or minimums which govern their very existence in the work force.
I think we should remind ourselves that minimum labour standards are designed to ensure that all workers, whether organized or not, who are employed by small businesses or large corporations are entitled to specific conditions of employment which conform to socially acceptable norms. These are designed to establish a legal barrier below which these conditions cannot be driven by the unfettered play of market forces.
At a time when those who plan the future shape of our system of social security are searching for comprehensive solutions to the problems of poverty, including those faced by the working poor, this barrier represented by minimum standards is being increasingly recognized as an important instrument of social policy. It is so recognized by the government of Canada and will be used accordingly.
Again let me remind the House, although I believe most members know this, that the first Labour (Standards) Code was brought into existence in the federal field in 1965. I do not think anyone would mind if I were to pay tribute to the present government House leader, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), who piloted through the House the first Labour (Standards) Code in 1965. I believe those of us who are preoccupied with portfolios which address themselves primarily to people will recognize that this original piece of legislation has made a valuable contribution to Canadian development, and I hope these amendments will make it an even more valuable piece of legislation.
As members may recall, the 1965 code covered certain basic standards governing hours of work, overtime pay, vacations with pay and general holidays. The minimum wage at the time was $1.25. The standard hours of work were set at eight per day and 40 per week with a maximum of 48 per week. The minimum rate for overtime beyond standard hours was set at time and one half, the minimum paid vacation at two weeks and the minimum number of paid general holidays at eight per year.
In the present bill we are introducing amendments that relate to all the standards which I have just enumerated. These amendments are based on the experience over the last five years and they are intended, for the most part,

April 26, 1971
Canada Labour (.Standards) Code to overcome many administrative problems and to avoid unnecessary interference with the practices established by collective bargaining. This is the result of the experience of five or six years during which the standards have been in force.
In addition to this, we intend, as hon. members who are familiar with the bill know, to introduce many new features to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code which are new at least in the federal field. My hope is that among other things these amendments will make it possible to deal more effectively with the type of difficulty that has made it necessary, in so far as the existing hours of work provisions are concerned, to issue special orders covering certain portions of the transportation industry and to keep railroads under deferment.
I think most hon. members appreciate the difficulty which we had in introducing the standards under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code in the field of transportation, the problem of adapting the code to the railway industry, the tracking industry, the airline industry and the shipping industry. Consequently, for six years a rigidity has been built into the existing legislation which has made it rather difficult, in the part of the code dealing with hours of work, to introduce the code with any consistency.
It is my intention to see that the increased flexibility which is proposed in this bill will permit me not only to make the bill more applicable and more functional in these areas but also to allow it to be used with good sense and in consultation with labour and management. In this way we will be able to ensure that the spirit of the code is applied both to employers and to employees in the transportation industry. With one obvious exception, and that is the minimum wage, there will be no basic change in the standards now set forth in the code. Measured against the norms established by international conventions, provincial laws and the provisions of collective agreements, these standards still appear to be appropriate as minimum standards.
With regard to minimum wages, hon. members may recall that some time before last July, if I am not mistaken, we amended the minimum wage provisions, or that portion of the Labour (Standards) Code that applied to minimum wages, to increase the minimum wage from $1.25 to $1.65 per hour. At the same time I promised the committee that I would recommend the increase of the minimum to $1.75 when I brought in the bill and that I would try to find ways and means of facilitating future adjustments to the minimum wage.
I think hon. members will recall that the minimum wage prior to last July had not been changed for five years, which meant that people who worked for minimum wages found not only their dollar eroding but that it was almost ludicrous and certainly a disincentive to work for the minimum wage of $1.25 per hour-$50 per week-which in many provinces is below the amount paid through welfare payments. What I propose to do in the bill is to make it possible to increase the minimum wage, preferably every year by Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Labour.
I think this will get us over the problem with which we were faced between 1965 and 1970 when certain events made it impossible to get around to raising the minimum wage by bringing legislation before the House. I believe there were one or two elections, just to mention one unexpected event which can impede the orderly increase of minimum wages. I believe that the ability to adjust minimum wages by Governor in Council will be a useful addition to the bill; and of course, once again this added power will be used judiciously.
As Minister of Labour I would provide for a continuing process of review in which representatives of employers and trade unions will be invited periodically to participate so that the minimum wage can be periodically revised and maintained at an economically relevant and socially desirable level. This was one of the subject matters that we discussed in the past week with Ministers of Labour from across Canada. The impact that federal minimum wages could or do have on the provinces and on their own particular norms is felt as the Ministers of Labour of the provinces realize the need to keep alive and in existence a labour incentive industry rather than a capital incentive industry.
In setting the federal rate we must at all times recognize the distortion that any change might have on the provinces. I might remind the House that the minimum applies only to employees of the age of 17 years and over, but since 1965 we have set a special rate by regulation for people in the work force under 17 and last July we raised that rate from $1 to $1.40 per hour. If the general minimum is increased as now proposed, I intend to recommend to my colleagues a similar increase to employees under 17 which would bring the minimum wage up to $1.50 per hour.
I think the government has made it clear that it recognizes the need to examine all aspects of law and policy which affect the rights of women in Canadian society. To this end it has launched a careful review of the many recommendations contained in the recent report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. I am pleased that the Department of Labour will be heavily involved in the review which will proceed in a climate that the work of our women's bureau has helped to create. I am also pleased that as Minister of Labour I can now come forward with legislative proposals that are consistent with the general thrust of the royal commission's recommendations. I refer, of course, to the provisions in the bill relating to equal pay for equal work, and maternity leave. Given the large and continuing increase in the number of women including married women who participate in the work force, it seems to me that these two basic provisions are essential.
The amendments to the act would replace the existing provisions of the Female Employees Equal Pay Act of 1956 by strengthened provisions in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. The proposed change of statutory locale is in itself important because in my opinion problems of inequity affecting women should wherever possible be dealt with, not in special legislation for women but in general legislation applicable to Canadians whether male or female. In this connection members of

April 26, 1971

the House will note that the language used in the proposed new equal pay part of the code will prohibit pay differentials based on sex, whether directed against men or against women.
The proposed new standard should be much more effective, for two reasons. To begin with, the prohibitive practice is more broadly defined, referring not to "identical or substantially identical work" but to "the same or similar work on jobs requiring the same or similar skill, effort and responsibility". Equally important, application of the law will no longer be dependent upon the receipt of complaints of individuals. The proposed new provisions will be subject to the general inspection and enforcement procedures of the code.
I think this is a very important change because under the existing legislation which has been around since 1956 the onus of responsibility for initiating a complaint or investigation rests with the person who feels she is aggrieved. Many women insecure in the work force dare not initiate such a complaint and therefore the act has not had nearly the impact that it should. Now that it is to be placed within the ambit of the Labour (Standards) Code, the responsibility will be broadened. Not only will the department act on complaints by women in the work force, but a complaint or an alleged violation of the act will be brought forward by the inspectors who will inspect the records of employers with respect to hours of work-something which they have been doing for some years. This added responsibility placed on the shoulders of the inspectors should do much to eliminate the discrimination which has gone on for far too long in the federal field.
The amendments relating to maternity leave would prohibit dismissal or lay-off solely because of pregnancy, and establish a right to maternity leave. An employee with at least one year of service would be entitled to maximum leave covering a period 11 weeks before and six weeks after delivery, together with any period between the estimated and actual dates of delivery. I hope that pleases some members of the New Democratic Party because I am not too sure that this type of legislation was pleasing to all members of that party at their convention last week.
I should note that the period of 11 weeks before and six weeks afterward is consistent with the provisions in the bill to revise the Unemployment Insurance Act under which an employee whose earnings are interrupted by pregnancy, after a two-week waiting period will be entitled to benefits for a maximum period of 15 weeks. The combined effect of these provisions will be that in most cases an employee who must take time off for the purposes of childbirth will be entitled both to job security and a reasonable level of income maintenance. I think hon. members will agree that this provision represents an important forward step.
There is another area that the Labour (Standards) Code deals with this time that was not in it in 1965. This concerns the increasing problem of people who are leaving the work force, of the senior worker who is forced
Canada Labour (Standards) Code out of his job through automation and who realizes that less and less he can depend entirely on seniority for security of tenure. I think we all agree that in this technological age this is one of the big problems faced by any worker-the problem of adjusting from one job to another, the shock of losing work and in some cases the shock for a person who finds that his or her skill is redundant. That person needs all the help that Parliament can extend, and this principle is quite consistent with the basic philosophy of all political parties.
In the bill there is provision in the case of large scale terminations for notice to the government and to any trade union representing the workers affected, the required period of notice varying from eight to 16 weeks depending on the size of the group terminated. The purpose of this provision is to ensure that there is time for employers and trade unions to work closely with the Department of Manpower and Immigration so that the placement, training and relocation services provided by that department can be brought fully into play. It is unfortunate that all too frequently large groups of people, particularly in the unorganized sector of the work force, are laid off with little or no advance notice, making it increasingly difficult for the Department of Manpower and Immigration to be effective and to guide them into other work if they have a particular skill and work is available.
In the case of people eligible for unemployment insurance, again this advance notice is of importance if there is to be no undue hardship suffered by the worker in applying for unemployment insurance. It is my hope and belief that the great majority of employers will be both willing and anxious to comply with the group notice requirements of the law. In the event that they do not, we will provide fines in the bill ranging up to $100,000. I would hope this would be sufficient deterrent to those employers who, by any stretch of the imagination, would want to ignore the provisions of the law which insist that there be sufficient notice for group termination of work.
The second standard in this general area would provide the individual whose employment is being terminated with entitlement to a minimum notice of two weeks or an equivalent amount of play in lieu of notice. The third standard that is new in the legislation, that we did not have before and which I think is equally important, is that for the first time we have introduced this feature for what you might call the unorganized sector, the feature of a legal right to a minimum amount of severance pay. I think that severance pay, grouped with the provision for advance notice of termination, is of tremendous significance in this particular field.
An employee with five years or more of service whose employment is being terminated, except by way of dismissal for just cause or retirement on an immediate pension, would be entitled to two days' pay for each year of service, up to a maximum of 40 days' pay. Assuming a five-day week, this would mean a minimum severance payment ranging from two weeks' pay for an employee with five years of service to eight weeks' pay for an employee with 20 or more years of service.

April 26, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
There is another amendment that would prohibit dismissal of an employee solely because he was the subject of garnishment proceedings. This may not seem significant but, ironically, many people are dismissed because they happen to be the subject of garnishment proceedings. I think it is unfortunate that so many employers, rather than be bothered with the paperwork associated with court orders simply prefer to dismiss an employee. I have never been able to understand the social sense of an employer who would do this, but from our statistics we know that it is a fairly common practice. When an employee is in financial difficulties he should not be subject to loss of employment and earnings simply because his employer must undertake the paperwork required to comply with a court order for garnishment of wages. Therefore, if Parliament approves this bill we would prohibit this practice and see it is brought to an end in industries within federal jurisdiction.
There are two other areas concerning the bill which I would like to mention. One is that under its provisions the new standards relating to equal pay for equal work, maternity leave, group terminations of employment and dismissal for garnishment would apply to managerial and professional employees as well as to all other employees. The original act, if I am not mistaken, set standards for a particular, identifiable group of employees spelled out in the act. What we are doing here is making these provisions relating to equal pay for equal work, maternity leave, group terminations of employment and dismissal for garnishment apply to managerial and professional employees just the same as to all other classes of workers. This is an important departure and in my view is fully justified in view of the social significance of the standards in question.
Hon. members who have read the bill will also have noted that for most of the amendments the proposed effective date is July 1, 1971. Because of the possibility that related regulations will require a somewhat longer period in which to prepare and discuss them with interested parties, it is proposed that the provisions relating to notice of termination of employment and severance pay should come into effect on a date to be fixed by proclamation, which will be the earliest possible date after July 1.
Again I remind hon. members that the Canada Labour (Standards) Code does not apply to the public service as a matter of law. However, as the result of a commitment made to Parliament in 1965 by the then Minister of Labour, the standards established by the code are applied to the public service as a matter of government policy. I am pleased to now reiterate that commitment with respect to the standards embodied in the proposed amend-mends.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, although in preparing the bill we have given careful consideration to the provisions of relevant conventions and recommendations of the International Labour Organization, the contents of related laws in the provinces, the provisions of collective agreements, the views expressed from time to time by labour and management and the experience of the department in administering the code, I am hoping the

bill will receive careful scrutiny by the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration and that the committee will agree to receive representations from the major organizations of employers and trade unions. I assure the House that constructive criticism and comment will be both welcome and carefully considered as the bill proceeds through the parliamentary process.
In my opinion and in the opinion of the government this is important legislation designed to benefit working men and women and deserves to be examined with care before taking its place on the statute books. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to move that Bill C-228, an act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, be read a second time.

I think it is important in this area
because it seems to me, as the minister has explained, that the vast bulk of our labouring force is within the unorganized field. Those who are affected by collective bargaining have an opportunity and, usually, the wherewithal with which to protect themselves, so it is within those areas that we have to be concerned about good leadership. I think the minister has indicated that through federal and provincial prerogative they can give some leadership to those who are not adequately protected.
What we are trying to do here, Mr. Speaker, is establish a social policy ranging from the study of the minimum wage to questions of discrimination and the establishment of safety codes. I know the minister believes this latter point is extremely important and I understand that legislation will be brought forward in keeping with its importance. I agree with what the minister has said, that this legislation effects a minimum wage, equal pay for equal work, maximum hours of work, maternity leave, giving notice of separation, and severance pay. All these are very important, timely and necessary. Of course, we reserve the right to question some of the matters raised by the legislation.
There are two important areas in which I believe the government's response is inadequate in light of crying social conditions. One is the provision for the adjustment of the minimum wage and the other is the bringing in of equal pay for equal work. I was impressed with what the minister said in attempting to bring before the House the position he takes regarding the provision for adjustment of the minimum wage. However, I was a little disappointed inasmuch as I was led to understand last fall, when the minister introduced legislation increasing the mini-
April 26, 1971

mum wage from $1.25 to $1.65, that he would attempt to bring in an adjustment procedure or standard. This has not occurred.
The minister indicated that he has met with his colleagues at the provincial level. I understand that they are to meet periodically to discuss the matter and if they feel the climate warrants it or the political atmosphere makes it desirable-this is what concerns me-the minister will move to increase the minimum wage. I shall discuss that matter shortly. When we are talking about guidelines in this area, I think it is important to realize that the minister's decision can be affected by political atmosphere, particularly when we see how this government moves-I say this with a great deal of respect-and when we realize their complacency or policy with respect to creating unemployment. It may mean that the minister cannot take the opportunity to raise the minimum wage.
I believe the hours of work provide for a 48-hour week, with exceptions in certain circumstances. We are desirous of having this bill go to committee because in this area we run into the whole problem of transportation. The minister is well aware of that problem. I understand that permits will continue to be granted with respect to exceptions to the 48-hour week in those industries or commercial endeavours which need an extension. 1 think it is advisable that guidelines be established and I am sure we will deal with this question in committee. The guidelines that are proposed should take into consideration the situation where a restricted work week of 48 hours will be detrimental to employers or employees and where the nature of the work would make the regulation unreasonable. We will have to discuss this point at some length.
I have discussed the minimum wage, but I was short of time when the minister increased it to $1.65 last year. He was not very happy because I think it had been stated by several people on his behalf that he was interested in making it at least $1.75 an hour. On a previous occasion I said that while there may be no absolute virtue in leaving the procedure for adjustment within the amending process of Parliament, the government had not proposed an alternative that really improved the existing procedure. If the minimum wage has as its objective a floor consistent with current needs, this objective should be pursued by means of an automatic adjusting factor which would keep it in line with the cost of living. That is what we proposed on this side and we thought the minister would be bringing it in. Perhaps there is an explanation so I shall not dwell on the matter except to state that such an adjustment would naturally bypass amendment in Parliament, and with the proposed amendment Parliament would be bypassed without the rationale of automatic adjustment. The amendment proposed does not even provide a broad guideline or formula upon which a cabinet decision would be based. I suggest that there is an unacceptable arbitrariness on the part of the cabinet when the minimum wage is to be changed.
The matter of equal pay for equal work I believe primarily stems from the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women and reflects the general attitude regarding the importance of women in the work force.

This is extremely important. When we talk about equal pay for equal work, the consistency of our thinking becomes extremely realistic and acceptable. The Economic Council has stated-

Yes, I am reading because I wrote it myself in the first instance. If you had been listening, my friend, instead of reading that paper you would have heard me say that I made a speech about the problems of women. By 1980, women will form a larger percentage of the national labour force than they did even in the man-short years of the second World War. It is obvious that this larger and more widespread employment of women will mean that they will wield an evermore direct influence upon national affairs and have an ever-increasing voice in Canada's destiny. Their interest, too, will grow more direct and less passive as they leave the restricted scope of the housewife for the wider field of industry and commerce, public life and public affairs.
The coming decade will inevitably be a decade of expansion and development for Canada-or so we hope. Up to the early sixties, Canadian women formed a smaller proportion of the national labour force than was the case in the six other leading western industrial states. But the Economic Council believes that during the seventies Canada will approach the levels of female participation prevailing in other leading industrial countries. This indicates pretty clearly that during the seventies Canadian women will achieve all they could wish in regard to participation in the nation's work force.

But what about the quality of the positions they will hold? What about progress up the ladder within the labour force? This is an old battleground. This is where a good deal of the masculine talk about the equality of women is shown to be merely lip-service to an abstract ideal rather than practical adherence to accepted custom.
In an address to the Beth Tzedec Sisterhood in Toronto last December, Miss Sylva M. Gelber, director of the women's bureau of the Canada Department of Labour-a woman for whom I have a great deal of respect-emphasized the inequalities and discrimination that face women who would enter the professions or business. I want to put on record the fact that I think Canadians are becoming more aware of the important role that women can play. In this regard I should like to refer to a poll conducted by the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion, published in the Ottawa Citizen for March 20 under the headline "Women getting support for rights, says poll". The following questions were asked:
Would you tell me it you approve or disapprove of these suggestions:
That women who work should receive equal pay with men for the same kind of work?
That, by law, women should be given leave of absence by their employers totalling 18 weeks for pregnancy and confinement?
Then follows a table showing public opinion. With regard to equal pay for women, 80 per cent of the people of Canada approved and only 11 per cent disapproved. The undecideds were 2 per cent.
In regard to the statements made by Miss Gelber, I might add that Mr. John Carson, chairman of the Public Service Commission, has called down the blame on his own head for discrimination against women in the federal bureaucracy, and I respect him for doing so. I hope the minister is aware that you cannot talk of motherhood and pay only lip-service to it. I think the minister must give the fair employment practices act sufficient teeth to do its job.
I should also like to quote some of the points made in a report in the Spectator for March 19 last:
Mr. Carson said the report last December of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women left the commissioners "desperately ashamed of ourselves"...
As for problems involving women workers, he said the commission is seeking to bring more women into its executive training program. The federal government employs 81,000 women, mostly in secretarial and clerical roles.
When the bill goes before the standing committee I hope the minister will make definitive statements regarding his recommendations to Mr. Carson, and the federal government's approach to this very vital and sensitive area. We all hear of the activities of Women's Lib and we have had the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. Unless the federal government shows leadership in bringing women into the work force in a way which means they are accepted for the contributions they make, instead of on the basis of just being women, we are going through an exercise in frustration at the present time.
However outstanding the merit of the progressive amendment regarding equal pay for equal work, I

respectfully state that the effect of this amendment is quickly nullified by the qualifying provision that follows, and I should like the minister to reflect on this. I refer to the proposed new section 14AC2) which reads:
Payment to male and female employees of different wages does not constitute a violation of subsection (1) if the difference is based on any factor or factors other than sex that justify such a difference.
It seems to me that this provision derogates from the initial intention of the equal pay for equal work legislation. This is precisely the kind of situation the commissioners had in mind when they recommended an improvement in the language describing an equal pay for equal work situation. While attempting to improve their credibility by making a linguistic leap of faith, the government has ensured, by this qualifier, that the real situation will remain the same as it was. I suggest this aspect must be carefully watched if we are to retain our credibility.
With regard to maternity leave, which we heard about in the white paper on unemployment insurance, I was under the impression that under the Unemployment Insurance Act the period was 15 weeks. There is now a two-week difference; the period under this legislation is 17 weeks.

We must also remember that once this legislation is on the books, it will not apply to all the workers of Canada. It will only apply to those who are in industries that come under federal labour jurisdiction. This represents about 10 per cent of the work force. Perhaps it is a little higher if the public servants who are brought in by regulation are included, but it is still a very small section of the labour force of this country. For this to be universal, it would require constant agitation in all the provincial legislatures in order to get those bodies to bring in comparable legislation. It is quite true that it is in this place that a lead can be given. I hope the improvements that are before us tonight in this legislation will be noted by the legislatures of all the provinces and that they will make similar improvements.

I might also add as another preliminary remark that what bothers me about this kind of legislation is the number of loopholes that are always to be found in it- the exceptions it contains. For a number of years, we have had the Canada Labour (Standards) Code on the books. That provides for a maximum of 40 hours of work per week at which time overtime is supposed to begin. There have been a succession of permits from Ministers of Labour that have excepted some employers from that part of the Labour (Standards) Code. I notice that there are some of these things in the bill now before us, Bill C-228.
In the interesting section about the termination of employment where more than 50 people are turfed out at once, while some things must be done-I will deal with them in a few minutes-the requirement to do this can be waived by the minister if in his opinion it would be injurious to a particular industry or to the public. I do not know why we have to mess up good pieces of legislation with all these exceptions.
It is always a matter of concern how long it takes to get the regulations passed that are necessary to put this kind of legislation fully into effect. As the minister knows, because he has had to answer questions of mine about it here and in other places, he has the companion piece of legislation known as the Canada Labour (Safety) Code. The minister will recall, because he was then just a lowly Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour, that in December 1966 the then Minister of Labour urged us to get that bill through. He said it was important to get the law on the statute books to enable the regulations to be made. After all, people were being hurt, people were losing their lives because safety provisions had not been established.
We co-operated with the then Minister of Labour and with the then parliamentary secretary, the present Minister of Labour, in getting that bill through. That was in December, 1966. Now, in April, 1971, the minister still cannot point to a complete set of regulations under that bill. Mind you, he did express confidence a few days ago, when I questioned him about the matter, that these regulations would be completed before the end of 1971.

I move on to some other features of this bill about which the minister and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) have been speaking. One which has been mentioned is the proposal to increase the minimum wage from $1.65 to $1.75 an hour. I wonder whether the Minister of Labour in his own way managed to arrange for this bill to be debated tonight on the same day the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that there would be an increase of $8,000 a year for ourselves. A minimum wage of $1.75 an hour for a 40-hour week would amount to $70, and for 50 weeks in a year, allowing for a couple of weeks' holiday, it would amount to $3,500 a year. Quite seriously, it seems to me that this is a different question altogether, whether the woman is hired at all. But if a woman is an employee and has a job, why should she not get the maternity leave if she has been employed only 51 weeks rather than 52? I think we can improve this provision when we get it before the standing committee.
Let me move on to that part of the bill which deals with termination of employment. These are new sections to be put into the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, and we welcome them. As the minister knows, this is another case of the government looking over private members' bills, seeing that there are good ideas in them and deciding to put them into legislation. The minister has picked up ideas from members on this side of the House quite often.
I notice that the provision regarding mass termination of employment really does not go much further than giving notice. You still lose your job. Granted, it is of some use for the Department of Labour, the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the trade unions to know it is happening. But is that enough? What about the whole question of pay? Perhaps the provisions in respect of two weeks' pay for individuals laid off, or severance pay for those with five years' service still apply in the case of mass lay-offs, but as I look at the bill this does not seem to be very clear.
Then I wonder why the minister has chosen the figure of 50. Why only if 50 or more are being laid off is this procedure to be complied with? It seems to me the figure should be much lower. I would make it as low as ten. If ten or more people are being laid off, this provision should be complied with. This area in the bill seems to have three main parts. There is the case of what happens if 50 or more people are laid off, and I said I believed it should be down to ten. Then there is the part which deals with individual employees being laid off who get two weeks' notice or pay in lieu of notice if they have been working for the same employer for three months. That is good and it has pretty well been taken out of bills presented from this side of the House. Then there is the other provision about severance pay which also is good. This, however, is allowed only in the case of employees who have been five years with the same employer.
We are in an age of great shifting around as a result of changes due to automation, computers and all the rest of it, and as time goes on this trend will probably be even more striking and the number of people who work for

employers for periods of less than five years will grow. I suggest the period should be much less than it is. The whole area in this bill having to do with termination of employment and severance pay is new. It is good. It was not put in when the President of the Privy Council brought in the legislation five or six years ago. Precisely because it is new I think it should be dressed up a bit and I hope we can deal with it appropriately in the standing committee.
In the statement he made this evening the minister said that the Canada Labour (Standards) Code covers a number of other things such as vacations with pay and general holidays, as well as one or two others. Then he said that although we are not changing the standards that are already in the legislation having to do with vacation pay and general holidays, some of the regulations are being changed. This is correct. I have looked over the bill and I see there are a number of instances in which definitions are being changed to make certain that employees get the two weeks' vacation a year provided in the legislation, general holidays, and so on. The minister is nodding to indicate that I am interpreting it correctly. But so far that is all the minister is doing in the bill with regard to vacations with pay and general holidays. Let me give him notice of amendments. We have brought in amendments before, and we can do it again. On occasion our amendments have even been accepted.
On the question of vacations with pay, when the hon. Michael Starr first brought in his bill it provided for one week's vacation after one year of service, and two weeks' vacation after two years or more of service. That did not seem to us to be good enough and we persuaded the Liberals when they returned to office to improve it so that it would be two weeks after the first year of service. It is slightly improved now. It is now two weeks for a year of service, so they do not get caught with the use of the word "after". There are some jurisdictions in this country where for longer service there is a longer vacation.
I have a bill on the order paper which I believe is a minimal proposal. It asks for vacation with pay of three weeks after three years' service. It is so little I am almost ashamed to be asking for it. An employee would have to work three years with the same employer before he would receive three weeks' vacation. At least, it is better than two weeks, and I say that no Labour (Standards) Code is worthy of the name if it does not have at least that minimum in it. I have a private member's bill which would provide for that. I do not know whether it will be reached this session, but if so it will be talked out, because that is the usual fate of such bills. I am grateful to the minister for bringing in this bill amending the Labour (Standards) Code, because in it he touches on the question of vacations with pay and I think this will give us an opportunity to move an amendment in the committee.
The same thing applies to the question of general holidays. The bill the President of the Privy Council brought in five or six years ago had a proposal in respect of seven general holidays. In the committee of the whole we were able to get an amendment through which
Canada Labour (Standards) Code provided an eighth holiday, Remembrance Day. The public service has more than eight general holidays in the course of a year, and there are some other areas of employment where this is also the case. It seems to me the time has come to increase the number to at least nine. I hope this is one of the improvements we will make to the legislation when the bill reaches the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
I see, Sir, that I have not used up all my time, but that is no reason to stay on my feet another five minutes. I am sure my valuable assistants in the back rows are itching to get to their feet, and also members in other parts of the House, so I shall resume my seat. If I have not been able to make the rafters ring about this legislation, I hope at least, with the assistance I have had from all sides of the House, I have been able to make my point.
I make the point as strongly as I can that we should not be satisfied just because we have a bill which makes a few improvements. It does that, and I give the minister all the credit he has already asked us to give him for doing it. But I say, why stop there? We do not amend the Labour (Standards) Code very often. Times now move a lot faster than they did when this type of legislation was first introduced. In view of the fast way in which times are moving, I hope we will make all the improvements in this bill which I have suggested when we get to the committee, and a few more so that when we come back and the minister rises to move third reading he will be able to say-I shall draft his little speech for him now- "It gave me a great deal of pleasure to introduce this bill for second reading, and it gives me infinitely more pleasure to move its third reading because the job the members in the committee have done has made it very much better."

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Labour (Standards) Code is the legislation establishing the minimum standards governing the basic conditions of employment in industries under federal jurisdiction. There are approximately 530,000 employees in the industries governed by the Code, whose standards also apply to the federal public service as a governmental policy.
The initial legislation of 1965 established the minimum standards governing salary rates, working hours, overtime pay, leave with pay and statutory holidays.
Under the current provisions of the Code, the bill proposes for the first time the creation of standards concerning maternity leave, notice of employment termination, severance pay and garnishment. It provides for major changes in existing standards with respect to the minimum wage and equal pay for equal work. It contains a number of other changes.

the minimum wage in the future. The normal duration of work is eight hours a day and 40 hours a week, with a maximum of 48 hours a week. The minimum rate applicable to work performed over and above normal working hours is half as much again as the normal rate.
Minimum annual leave is set at two weeks per year, and the minimum number of legal holidays with pay is eight per year.
Representatives of the Department of Labour would have to watch very closely the terms of the application of the act and regulations. One only has to look at the list of the employers who have asked that the application of the Labour Code to their organization be delayed, to understand what I am referring to.
Close to five years after the passing of the act in Parliament, there still are workers who are required to work a weekly number of hours which go far beyond the provisions of the Code and there are still too many employers who are reluctant to effect salary adjustments.
I could quote various instances with regard to employees of the CNR, especially those extra gangs doing seasonal work on branch-line construction or road repairs. Indeed, the number of hours worked does not always comply with the requirements of the Code.
The industries to which the Code applies are, I think, the railroads, truck transportation, pipeline construction, water transportation and other key services relating to water transportation of an interprovincial or international character; air transportation, interprovincial or international telephone, telegraph and cable systems, radio, television and banks.
Establishing a minimum wage level and standard hours of work does not result from collective bargaining involving employees of a given industry or service. It is however quite normal to link to such a minimum wage factors which cannot be ingored, such as cost of living, income of the worker and his ability to provide his dependents with a decent style of living, should he assume the responsibilities of a family.
Quite clearly, the rate of $1.75 per hour is inadequate. However, the adjustments of wage rates provided in Bill C-228 can serve as an example to provinces where the minimum wage is lower than $1.75 per hour. The minimum hourly wage set up in the various provinces in Canada varies between 85 cents and $1.50, except where there have been adjustments. The highest level in force is in British Columbia and the lowest in Newfoundland, namely $1.10 for men and 85 cents for women, which is ridiculous in 1971.
I am very happy to see that Bill C-228 provides for periodical reviews of minimum wage taking into account, I trust, economic fluctuations such as the cost of living, the devaluation of money or other factors that reduce the worker's purchasing power.
It would no doubt be profitable to the legislators to examine their conscience which would allow them to realize that the workers' claims are often inspired by example given them in various places.
As they note that fairly substantial salary raises are obtained in high places without any slow bargaining nor
detrimental strikes, which people try to justify by put-ing forward the constant increase in the cost of living, workers are inevitably led to wonder why there is so much tendency to niggardliness when it comes to ensure them a salary which will allow them and their families a decent living.
When the employees of the Canadian National, particularly those who have no adequate salaries and working conditions, note that a group of public servants travel in special cars built at a cost of half a million dollars or more, they are incensed. These cars which are extremely comfortable and furnished most luxuriously are used regularly by one group of officials on their travels, whether short or long, where they are joined by friends who take part in the treat, and this at the expense of the Canadian people who will pay in the end for these festivities taking place in picnic cars where the variety of bottles would make Bacchus himself jealous. These are luxury trips, at the expense of the taxpayers.
Should such special car service be discontinued, nearly four to five million dollars would be saved each year.
When workers realize that the railway president is earning $75,000 a year and that on retirement he is going to receive a $26,000 pension, they are certainly justified in demanding normal working conditions-at least those who look after track maintenance-and more suitable accommodations after an exhausting day of work. Bunks are no longer adequate in an era of research within the field of comfort.
I give that example to show that too often privileged people seem to forget the worries of workers who are often compelled to put up with working conditions which could be greatly improved. I could give a great many more examples of that kind. Obviously, a large number of grievances are sometimes quite difficult to solve.
Some responsible people have carried out investigations in different services and their reports show that not only have they determined the causes of certain problems but they have also offered suggestions that should be of help to the legislators when legislative measures establishing the rights of both employers and employees are to be amended or adopted. Some hon. members have had experience with the problems of workers and so their views should be taken under consideration without partisanship and at the right moment in order to correct the intolerable situation reflected in a series of strikes which, in most cases, are prejudicial to the workers, and which always have an unfavourable effect because they spread economic disorder.
This trend toward centralization often makes one forget about the efficiency of human communications which are required for appreciating employee's grievances. An ever-alert consultation mechanism must necessarily be created and maintained, especially when changes must be introduced in working conditions. Sacrificing the morale and well-being of employees to an ideal of efficiency or service is not normal.

April 26, 1971

Some important factors must be taken into account when working conditions have to be established. One must not lose sight of the fact that the employee is a human being and not a machine, that he seeks security and stability. He generally wants his working place to be well organized and managed and it is only right that he be treated in all fairness. The employee also wants to be informed about the state of his company's business, which makes him sure that he can expect a fair income.
Those are basic realities about the human being, that an active labour relations service must try to understand and correct, if required. In order to do so, we shall have to come to grips with a difficult problem because this is a purely abstract matter which covers the attitude of people, their motivations, interests, fears, personal problems and what is most flexible, the human being. However, if everyone tries to understand his role, it is highly possible that all those concerned will reach agreement as they would all like to.
Following industrialization, workers have pratically become proletarians and they were forced to sacrifice to big undertak.ngs their legitimate desire to be their own masters, as yesterday's economy allowed them to be.
Therefore it seems that modern industry should provide workers with some compensation for the sacrifices they endure and for the alienation of their freedom.
Workers have less security than they had before. Technology, automation and competition between producers constantly threaten them with unemployment, its miseries and privations. The worker therefore feels dispossessed, and becomes bitter, specially when he realizes that big industry subordinates the fate of the worker to efficiency, that is to the return on its capital.
The word "dialogue" is very much in fashion in our modern society. It means that people with differing opinions have the opportunity of exchanging views with others. Still, the real problem lies with persuading each one of the parties to listen to the ideas of the other, then to revise and question his own. Perhaps we should adopt as a slogan to speak less and listen more! When everyone speaks at once and no one listens, there is no communication, only noise.
In this chamber the rules state that only one member may have the floor at a time. However, this does not always establish a communication of ideas. In a corporation, we see that if the boss does not listen to the workers, the workers will not listen to the boss. If university administrators do not listen to the students, the students will not listen to the administrators.
And if the government does not listen to the representatives of industry, industry will not listen to the government's representatives. Often it happens that the government and labour do not speak the same language, especially when talking about the government's wage policy and the workers.
These are terms that many people use with different connotations. I recently came upon an editorial written by Mr. Jean-Paul Desbiens in the March 31, 1971 issue of
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
La Presse; this article is quite appropriate to the circumstances. It says:
The need for rationalization leads on the one hand to centralization and, on the other, to longer and longer collective agreements. Contrarily to living beings, collective agreements never discharge any waste. Moreover, negotiators-whichever side of the table they may sit on-tend to develop the habit of endlessly polishing old clauses while inventing new ones. All parties argue about where a comma should be placed and run the risk of forgetting the basic aim of collective agrements, namely to humanize labour relations.
In fact, relations become more and more entangled in formality and pettifogging. Instead of mapping a safety zone for everybody, collective agreements become a mine field.
Nobody realizes how beneficial it would be to administer a good purgative to the old collective agreements. After all, collective agreements are not unlike pharmacies: about three quarters of the pills could well go down the drain without the citizens being affected in their health.
It is unfortunate to note sometimes that people who should be interested in maintaining good relations are not as anxious to fulfill their responsibilities as they are to claim their rights. Many problems would automatically be solved if people were more concerned about putting into practice that good old law of compensation which says that well-done work should be rewarded. With the new production methods used in this age of automation, a good number of workers are prone to demand high pay for little work, with the result that in the different administrative services, there are function-holders who are not "functioning". Some could be compared to the big books in a library, the higher ones being often the ones that are used less.
I cannot help quoting the conclusions of a humourous observer, published in a newspaper, where he gave the best way of testing the reactions of an inanimate civil servant. The article was published on September 7, 1969 under the title "Dead or Asleep" and I quote:
As many service directors in the Public Service find it hard to know whether some public servants are dead or merely asleep, they issued the following memorandum: "Any public servant found seated after his death shall be summarily struck off strength in accordance with Rule 3043, paragraph P, section 8. On account of the great sensitiveness of our employees and of the great resemblance between death and their usual position, the inquiry must be made quietly so as not to wake up the employee, should he be merely asleep. If, after the inquiry, there is any doubt about the employee's condition, hand him a cheque. Should there be no reaction, it means he is dead. In some cases, the stretching hand instinct is so great that a post mortem spasm could occur. Be careful not to be misled.
To those who are under the impression that all problems, such as salary adjustments, unemployment insurance benefits and others can be solved through a computer, allow me to quote in conclusion the point of view of a contemporary observer:
A modem computer is an electronic wonder that makes extremely complicated mathematical operations in one ten-thousandth of a second and sends its results ten days too late.
I wish also to add that I support the passing of Bill C-228, as it is a step toward improvement and 1 have good reasons to believe that its study in committee will contribute to the clarification of its content.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate and to give my unqualified support to second reading of Bill C-228. This bill is an indication of the government's concern for the workingman. I am pleased to note that not only are we improving the present legislation but are branching out into a new field, namely, legislation providing for severance pay. I am sorry that time will not permit me to touch upon every area covered by the bill. Circumstances limit me to commenting on only one or two areas. However, from looking over the bill one cannot help conceding that it is legislation with which parliament should be concerned and should be happy to support.
.50 p.m.)
As a former lawyer, I welcome the proposed amendment which would prohibit an employer dismissing, suspending or laying-off an employee solely on the ground that garnishment procedures have been or may be taken in regard to the employee's wages. It was inconceivable to me that an employer, because he was put to some additional bookkeeping, would see fit to terminate a man's employment because his wages had been garnisheed. In many cases the garnishee was not warranted nor, in fact, was it allowed by the court. Quite often the threat only that a garnishee proceeding might be taken would force debtors into a position of entering into unconscionable transactions in order to protect their jobs. I am pleased the government has seen fit to remove this form of legal blackmail which has been too readily available to creditors.
Mr. Speaker, I now want to say something about the proposed federal standard dealing with severance pay. It is my understanding that there is no existing federal or provincial legislation in respect of severance pay. It would be my guess-I do not have the statistics-that a large percentage of employees working under major collective agreements in Canada are covered by severance pay plans of some kind. It would also be my prediction that the proportion is almost certain to increase because of the interest in job security that is manifesting itself.
