maintopic: OIL-PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION-PARTICIPATION BY BRITISH COLUMBIA IN MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
OIL-PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN OPPOSITION-PARTICIPATION BY BRITISH COLUMBIA IN MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without question one of the most important issues facing Canada today concerns the manner in which another country is moving oil from one part of its domain, namely, Alaska, to the great markets of the southern portion of the United States. This question concerns the protection of the ecological heritage of this country, it impinges on considerations of our political sovereignty and it has significance in consideration of our own natural resources and our commercial politics and postures generally.
It is regrettable that in dealing with so vital a matter of concern to our own and succeeding generations the government of Canada displays a lack of purpose, a lack of consistency, a lack of vigour and at times, one fears, a lack of concern. We are advised that on May 3 a meeting is to be held with United States authorities on the matter. But what will the Canadian representative say at that meeting? What view or views will be presented or represented? When I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 21 if there was a cabinet-wide position on the TAPS route, he replied immediately, "No, Mr. Speaker, the subject has not been the object of policy by the government." So if the government has no policy-and this I readily believe-what will be the role of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) at this major meeting?
From various ministers we have had a wide spectrum of views. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has declared that he wants the TAPS route rejected. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) ponders aloud as to the right of Canada even to question the American gov-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
emment on the movement of oil down our west coast, considering tanker movements on our own east coast. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), and that ebullient, effervescent gentleman the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) go awooing American big business, suggesting that the Mackenzie Valley route is the best of all possible solutions. But the Minister of Communications, (Mr. Kierans), not one of the silent, strong members of the cabinet as is the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) at the moment, declares that a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley would be a disaster. Out of all this array of variance, uncertainty and contradiction, how can anyone believe that there could be coherence or consistency on this vital question among the group ox people now in charge of this nation's affairs?
I suggested to the Prime Minister the other day that since the British Columbia government and legislature had a clear point of view on this matter-unlike the government of Canada-steps should be taken to have the British Columbia government represented at the May 3 meeting. Then at least the people of British Columbia and the rest of the country would have some assurance that someone at least knew what they supported and knew what they opposed.
The danger of ecolocatastrophe on our west coast should be sufficiently frightening to stir the government into united action and strong representation to the United States authorities. I hope that after all the weeks and months of vacillation, contradiction, uncertainty and pusillanimous utterances, such a policy and such a voice will be forthcoming in time.
Mr. Barney Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to respond to the question posed by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) who has expressed concern about this rather important problem. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has expressed the government's very serious concern about the risk of pollution if the Alaska route is adopted. It was for this reason that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) requested consultation with United States officials, and as the hon. member has stated this will take place in Washington on May 3.
We have been in touch with the government of British Columbia on this question and it has been established that British Columbia officials will be participating in the Canadian delegation. This will also include officials from the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Transport and the Department of Fisheries and Forestry.
The consultations are on the problem of pollution and will deal with such matters as conditions relating to navigation, volume of oil which should be moved, drift in case of accident, effect on marine life, legislation and financial considerations. The Canadian interest is to prevent any damage to the natural environment more than with the problem of how we should clean up oil spills once they occur. We are seeking facts. There is a legitimate worry about the danger which a massive movement of oil would present to the natural environment. It is important that full information be assessed before action is taken which could prove detrimental to both countries.

April 26, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The hon. member suggests that there is no policy. There is no policy by the "seat of the pants". This government does not make policy in that way. Its concerns are deep and long-range. The hoped-for establishment of a ministry of the environment is a true indication of the government's concern in this area, together with the designation of one of the most able ministers ever to serve this country as minister of that department. So I think lack of coherence, consistency or concern, to use the hon. member's own words, does not exist. This is a time for thoughtful consideration, for consultation and for positive action stemming from well thought-out policies; and I think the hon. member will find that this will be the case.

maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE-ALLEGED PREFERENTIAL SALARY   TREATMENT FOR TORONTO EMPLOYEES COMPARED WITH QUEBEC
PUBLIC SERVICE-DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE-ALLEGED PREFERENTIAL SALARY   TREATMENT FOR TORONTO EMPLOYEES COMPARED WITH QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday April 21, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) the following question as recorded on page 5118 of Hansard:
Is the hon. minister aware of serious complaints lodged by federal civil servants employed in the family allowance branch in Quebec City, to the eifect that because of the department's practice of classifying employees doing the same kind of work, the officers on duty in the Toronto office receive $1,000 more annually than those in Quebec City?
I asked this question because in the Quebec region, we are always astonished at the difference between salaries paid by this department to its Toronto officers and those paid to the Quebec officers who belong to the same category.
This has already caused some protests on the part of the Quebec officers who know their rights are not respected.
At that time, prior to the integration into this department of certain employees of the Department of Supply and Services, the Quebec officer working in the "transfer" unit was classified CR 2 with a salary of $4,900 whereas an officer with the same position in Toronto was classified CR 3 with an additional $1,000 per year.
The Quebec officers lived through a moment of hope when the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated his election program in 1968, namely the establishment of a just society.
Perhaps the Prime Minister found pleasure in detailing his program. However, I think time has come to point out that the situation is still deplorable for the Quebec officers who are disgusted and tired of paying for other people.
Does the minister know that this kind of operation enabled the Quebec City office to record an administration surplus of $107,000 for the year 1969-70 and that this amount was transferred to Toronto, enabling the local office to grant salaries as those I have already mentioned?
Did the department give instructions to that effect or was there an understanding involving both offices exclusively? Why does the reclassification revision office tolerate such an injustice? How can the revision officers allow themselves to act in a way that leads us to question their ability and their intentions?
Does the minister know that two people went to the Quebec City office to inquire after the employees had informed of their grievances the former union leader the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand)?
Can the minister explain why the report that was to follow the inquiry was never made available to the interested parties?
Does the minister recognize the principle of equality: equal work, equal pay?
Can the minister tell us whether he intends to take into consideration the greater merit of the Quebec City office employees, who are bilingual and can therefore discharge their duties more quickly than their Toronto counterparts who must wait for the return of their correspondence which is translated through a special service?
I doubt that the minister is in possession of all the necessary information that would enable him to reply satisfactorily, since I am convinced that many things have been hidden from him until now. Therefore, I beg leave to suggest to the minister not to try and wash his hands of this business as Pilate once did.
This is too serious a question for me to expect a final answer today. In my view, this matter should be studied in depth. May I take the liberty of advising the minister on the choice of the investigators. He might prove to us his wish to really solve this problem in conducting a personal investigation which, all in all, should only require a few days, provided he contacts the people affected by this monkey business.
The best report could be prepared with co-operation of the victims of this hanky-panky, that is employees of all levels in the Quebec City office, who are in a position to provide him with all the details on this unfortunate situation.
If the Department of National Health and Welfare recognizes that family allowances and old age pensions should be paid at the same rate for both Quebec and Ontario residents, I submit that the minister should also recognize the need for paying the same salaries to his employees who operate under a classification which I feel should be the same throughout Canada.

NATIONAL PARKS-SHIP HARBOUR-PREVENTION OF LAND SPECULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to thank the minister for having stayed this evening. The issue I wish to bring forward arises from two brief questions I put to him, as reported in Hansard on April 21 on page 5122, having to do with reports and suggestions which are reaching my office in considerable numbers expressing concern and alarm over what appears to be land speculation in connection with a proposed park at Ship Harbour.
My purpose in being here tonight is to illicit certain information from the minister, not necessarily to emphasize the aspect I have just mentioned. I am sure that if there is anything of that nature going on, the minister and the federal authority will take steps accordingly, even though at this stage it would not be a matter of particular concern to them directly but one of indirect concern.
I should like to ask the hon. gentleman one or two simple questions. The answers to them, or the reaction to them, would go a long way toward bringing to an end the concern which arises when people are not kept advised of a situation. The first question is this: Why has there not been any form of communication with the public in the area concerned, in a public way, for more than a year? About a year ago the citizens of the area became sufficiently concerned to cause a public meeting to be held. Certain public officials attended that meeting and as a result a good deal of misunderstanding was cleared up. A year has now gone by and no attempt has been made to repeat this process.
My second question arises from the general vagueness which seems to surround the question of a third national park in Nova Scotia. There has been a clear indication in correspondence and from the provincial authorities that there will indeed be a third park in the province and that planning is in progress, but as yet there has been no public announcement by the minister to the effect that the federal authority has decided to go ahead. I think the minister should first call a meeting and, second, inform us whether it is intended to provide a park. He should have the common sense to tell the people in the area concerned what the boundaries are to be. This is the only
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion way in which it is possible to establish a park with minimum disruption to the people directly concerned and with minimum benefit to those who might use information, possibly coming from provincial offices, for their own advantage. This could put them in the position where they would go around the countryside buying up land they knew, or had reason to believe, the provincial government might buy for the purpose of developing a park. Some indication from the minister about these three very brief points would be very welcome.
